# repoarch 🗺️ **Turn any codebase into beautiful architecture diagrams — one command, no AI, no server, runs on any laptop.** Drop in a folder, get a clean, shareable architecture map. **Zero dependencies. Pure Python stdlib.** Works offline on a Raspberry Pi, a 2015 laptop, or a cloud VM — Mermaid + self-contained HTML that opens in any browser.

↓ generated from the sample/ project in this repo, in < 1 second ↓

--- ## ✨ Features | | | |---|---| | 🗂️ **4 output formats** | interactive `HTML`, `Mermaid .mmd`, `Graphviz .dot`, structured `JSON` | | 🌍 **14 languages** | Python · Go · JS/TS · Java · Rust · Ruby · PHP · C/C++ · C# · Kotlin · Swift · Dart | | 📊 **Graph metrics** | density, average degree, and core/backbone component ranking | | ⚙️ **Config file** | `.repoarch` for repeatable, project-specific runs | | 🔍 **Smart scanning** | gitignore-aware, `--exclude`, `--lang`, `--min-degree` filters | | 🎛️ **Flow control** | `LR` / `TB` / `RL` / `BT` layout, plus live edit + fullscreen in HTML | | 🤖 **Agent-ready** | installs as a skill for Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode | | 💸 **100% free** | zero dependencies, no AI, no server, no API keys, runs on any laptop | ## ✨ Why repoarch - **No AI.** No API keys. No paid services. Runs offline forever — your code never leaves your machine. - **No server.** Output is a **single self-contained HTML file** you can email, open, or host anywhere. - **Zero dependencies.** Pure Python standard library — installs in literally one command, works everywhere. - **Any language.** Python, Go, JS/TS, Java, Rust, Ruby, PHP, C/C++, C# — detected automatically. - **Instant.** Scans and renders a project in under a second. - **Agent-friendly.** Works great as a tool for Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. ## 🔧 Install ```bash # one line, no dependencies pip install repoarch ``` Or run without installing anything: ```bash # clone this repo, then: python -m repoarch /path/to/your/codebase ``` ## 🐳 Docker Pre-built images are published to the [GitHub Container Registry](https://github.com/users/dsk-dev-ai/packages/container/package/repoarch) (`ghcr.io/dsk-dev-ai/repoarch`) on every release. Pull, point it at any folder, and never install Python: ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/dsk-dev-ai/repoarch:1.0.0 # or :latest # map a folder to ./out and read the HTML docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" \ ghcr.io/dsk-dev-ai/repoarch:latest /app -o /app/out # -> /app/out/architecture.html ``` ## 🤖 Agent skill (Cursor · Claude Code · Codex · OpenCode) Works as a first-class skill in your favorite AI coding agent — ask it to "map this repo" and get a verified architecture diagram. ```bash # one-command install for all agents (or: cli, cursor, claude, codex, opencode) ./install.sh all # or use archify-style agent skill install npx skills add dsk-dev-ai/repoarch ``` Then just tell your agent: ```text Use repoarch to map this repository's architecture. ``` ## 🚀 Quick start ```bash # generate diagrams for any folder repoarch /path/to/codebase -o out/ # open the result in your browser open out/architecture.html # macOS xdg-open out/architecture.html # Linux start out/architecture.html # Windows ``` Output: | File | What it is | |---|---| | `architecture.html` | Interactive, self-contained diagram (dark/light, zoom, live edit) | | `architecture.mmd` | Raw [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org) source | | `architecture.dot` | [Graphviz](https://graphviz.org) `dot` source for external tools | | `architecture.json` | Structured component / edge / metric metadata | ## 🛠️ Options ```bash repoarch path [options] ``` | Flag | Description | |---|---| | `-o, --output` | Where to write the files (default: `.`) | | `--name` | Custom diagram title (default: folder name) | | `--min-degree N` | Hide low-importance components to declutter large projects | | `-x, --exclude` | Path(s) to exclude (repeatable), e.g. `-x tests -x docs` | | `--lang` | Only include these languages (repeatable), e.g. `--lang python --lang go` | | `-d, --direction` | Flow direction: `LR` (default), `TB`, `RL`, `BT` | | `--format` | Outputs to write: `all` (default), `html`, `mmd`, `json`, `dot` | | `-c, --config` | Path to a `.repoarch` config file (auto-detected by default) | | `--no-gitignore` | Do not honor `.gitignore` during the scan | | `--json` | Write `architecture.json` metadata (implied by `--format json/all`) | | `--version` | Print version and exit | ### Example ```bash # plot only Python + Go, left-to-right, include metrics repoarch ./myapp -o out --lang python --lang go -d LR --format all # use a config file, declutter repoarch ./bigrepo -c .repoarch --min-degree 2 ``` ## 🧠 How it works 1. **Scan** — walks the folder, skips `.git`, `node_modules`, `venv`, and other noise. 2. **Classify** — detects the language of every source file by extension. 3. **Extract** — parses `import` / `require` / `using` statements per language (regex, stdlib only). 4. **Group** — maps files to top-level components. 5. **Score** — ranks components by how central they are to the system. 6. **Render** — emits Mermaid + a self-contained HTML viewer. ## 🗺️ Language support Python · Go · JavaScript · TypeScript · Java · Rust · Ruby · PHP · C · C++ · C# · Kotlin · Swift · Dart ## 📊 Metrics With `--format all` or `--json`, repoarch reports graph metrics in `architecture.json`: - **Density** — how connected the module graph is - **Average degree** — mean in/out edges per component - **Core components** — the modules with the most relationships (your real architecture backbone) - **Top components** — ranked by importance ## 🤝 Contributing Issues, pull requests, and real-world diagrams are welcome. Want to add a language? It's one entry in `repoarch/parser.py`. ## ❤️ Sponsors repoarch is free, open source, and has **zero dependencies and zero running costs** to stay that way. If it saves you time, consider [sponsoring the project](https://github.com/sponsors/dsk-dev-ai) — every bit helps keep it free forever.

Support free, local-first dev tools
> Want to sponsor repoarch or list your product here? [Open an issue](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/repoarch/issues). ## ⭐ Support If repoarch saved you an hour of diagram-drawing, **give it a star** ⭐ — it helps more developers find it. ## 📄 License [MIT](LICENSE) — free to use, modify, and distribute.

# textrieve ### Image & PDF → text, free & fully open source. Drop in an image or a PDF — get clean text. **Offline OCR** on your own CPU, with a CLI, a REST API, and a polished browser UI. No accounts, no API keys, no paywalls, nothing stored server-side. [![Try it live](https://img.shields.io/badge/Try_it_live-textrieve.onrender.com-34d399?style=for-the-badge&logo=render&logoColor=white)](https://textrieve.onrender.com) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/textrieve?style=for-the-badge&logo=pypi&logoColor=white&color=3775a9)](https://pypi.org/project/textrieve/) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve?style=for-the-badge&logo=github&color=6c8cff)](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve?style=for-the-badge&color=0ea5e9)](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve/releases) [![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.10%2B-3178c6?style=for-the-badge&logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://www.python.org) [![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-009688?style=for-the-badge&logo=fastapi&logoColor=white)](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve/ci.yml?branch=main&style=for-the-badge&logo=githubactions&label=CI)](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve/actions) [![Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache--2.0-6c8cff?style=for-the-badge)](LICENSE)
> **Status:** v1.2.1 — multi-page **PDF → text**, language hints, auto-expiring results (2 min), live progress bar. Live on PyPI. > **Hosted:** [textrieve.onrender.com](https://textrieve.onrender.com) — UI + REST API on one free instance. --- ## Why textrieve? | Pain point | textrieve solves it | | --- | --- | | Paid OCR APIs, usage quotas | **100% free** — RapidOCR (ONNX) runs locally, MIT-licensed engine, bundled models | | Privacy leaks to third parties | Images never leave your machine / server — **no telemetry, no storage** | | Account walls & signups | No accounts. `pip install`, run, done. | | Janky one-off tools | A **real web UI**, a REST API, **and** a CLI in one repo | --- ## Contents - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Web UI](#web-ui) - [REST API](#rest-api) - [CLI](#cli) - [Privacy & auto-expiry](#privacy--auto-expiry) - [Free-tier deployment](#free-tier-deployment) - [Memory management](#memory-management) - [Tests](#tests) - [Roadmap](#roadmap) - [Support](#support) --- ## Quickstart **From PyPI:** ```bash pip install textrieve textrieve scan.png # image textrieve big.pdf --lang en # PDF ``` **From source:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve cd textrieve python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 ``` Open http://localhost:8080. --- ## Web UI Drag and drop an image or PDF (or click to browse) → preview → **Extract text** → copy or download. - Dark, responsive interface — works on desktop and mobile - Live **progress bar** (percent + elapsed time) while text is extracted - PDFs are extracted **page-by-page**, each one labelled `[Page N]` - Live **2-minute countdown** on results; the page is wiped clean automatically - Engine status indicator in the header; GitHub + Sponsor links in the footer - No cookies, no tracking pixels, no third-party scripts --- ## REST API | Method | Endpoint | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `GET` | `/api/health` | App version, OCR engine, live concurrency stats | | `POST` | `/api/ocr` | Multipart `file` upload → text + confidence + timing | ```bash curl -F "file=@photo.png" http://localhost:8080/api/ocr curl -F "file=@scan.pdf" "http://localhost:8080/api/ocr?lang=en" # PDF, language hint ``` ```json { "text": "HELLO TEXTRIEVE 2026", "confidence": 97.5, "engine": "RapidOCR (ONNX, CPU)", "duration_ms": 231.4 } ``` For PDFs the response also includes `"pages"` and the text is split with `[Page N]` markers. The optional `lang` query hints the OCR engine (e.g. `en`, `ch`, `japan`, `korea`). **Limits (free-tier friendly):** PNG / JPG / WEBP / BMP / TIFF / PDF · up to 12 MB · up to 25 PDF pages · oversize or bad-type uploads rejected with clear HTTP errors (415 / 413 / 503 under load). > **PDFs on the free hosted tier are slow:** pages are OCR'd one-by-one at roughly 30–60 s per > page on Render's free CPU. A 1–2 page scan fits fine; bigger documents should be split or OCR'd > locally (`pip install textrieve; textrieve big.pdf`). --- ## CLI ```bash python cli.py scans/receipt.jpg # print extracted text python cli.py scan.pdf --lang en # OCR a PDF, hint the language python cli.py a.png b.png --json # machine-readable output python cli.py ./documents/ # OCR every image/PDF in a folder ``` --- ## Privacy & auto-expiry - **Server-side:** each request is decoded, processed in memory, then released. Results are **never stored** — no database, no cache of extracted text. - **Client-side:** extracted text is **automatically erased 2 minutes** after extraction (live countdown shown). Closing the tab clears everything. - **Zero tracking:** no analytics scripts, no fingerprinting. --- ## Free-tier deployment One free Render instance hosts **both** the web UI and the REST API — a static front-end isn't needed. ### Render (UI + API in one service) ``` # 1. Use the included render.yaml # 2. New → Blueprint → connect this repo → Deploy ``` Or manually: build `pip install -r requirements.txt`, start `uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT --workers 1`, health check at `/api/health`. `render.yaml` and a `Dockerfile` are included; the health check keeps the free instance awake longer and restarts it cleanly after the idle timeout. The UI is plain HTML/CSS/JS served by FastAPI — the front-end talks to the OCR API on the same origin. **One-click deploy** (free tier): [![Deploy to Render](https://img.shields.io/badge/Deploy_to-Render-46e3b7?style=for-the-badge&logo=render&logoColor=white)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/textrieve) > **Honest note:** on Render's free tier a single CPU does roughly a few OCR passes per second > max. The built-in concurrency guards (2 parallel inferences, bounded queue) keep it alive > under bursts rather than letting memory pile up — a 1000-request/second crowd needs a paid > instance, but a 1000+ **users** day flows through one free box fine. Free instances also spin > down after ~15 minutes idle; the UI auto-retries the first cold request. --- ## Memory management Optional — included by default: - `ocr.py` releases the decoded image array immediately after inference and runs periodic GC - Images larger than 4000 px or 4 Mpx are downscaled before OCR - `app.py` limits concurrent ONNX inference to **2** and refuses (503) past a bounded queue — the process stays under ~512 MB on a busy day --- ## Tests ```bash python -m pytest -q ``` The suite **generates its own fixture files** (no external sample downloads) and covers: health, UI + favicon serving, real image and multi-page PDF OCR round-trips with confidence, blank images, invalid/missing/oversized uploads, and CLI loading. Gated in CI (GitHub Actions, Python 3.11/3.12). --- ## Roadmap - [ ] Batch queue in the web UI - [ ] PaddleOCR engine switch (even higher accuracy) - [ ] Searchable PDF export (text layer baked in) --- ## Support Built by [@dsk-dev-ai](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai). If textrieve saves you time, sponsor the project: [![Sponsor](https://img.shields.io/badge/Sponsor-GitHub%20Sponsors-34d399?style=for-the-badge&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sponsors/dsk-dev-ai) --- ## License [Apache-2.0](LICENSE). The RapidOCR engine is MIT-licensed; its ONNX models are distributed on an Apache-2.0 basis.

🧬 GenomeAI

Open-source AI platform for genomics, bioinformatics, biomedical research,
and evidence-based AI powered by public scientific databases and multi-provider LLMs.

## 🚀 Live Demo > **Try GenomeAI right now — no install required.** Click the link and use the > working application:

🌐 Open the Live Demo → https://genomeai.vercel.app
Backend API: https://genomeai-api.onrender.com · free-tier hosts, deployed automatically on every release. See docs/deployment/releases.md for how it works.

--- ## What is GenomeAI? GenomeAI is a unified platform that brings together **public biological databases**, **workflow automation**, **data visualization**, and **AI-powered analysis** — all in one open-source stack. It connects directly to **18 free public APIs** (NCBI, Ensembl, UniProt, ClinVar, gnomAD, PDB, AlphaFold, ChEMBL, PubChem, Reactome, KEGG, STRING, OpenTargets, Monarch, Disease Ontology, DGIdb, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar) to give researchers instant access to genomic, proteomic, chemical, and clinical data — without expensive licenses or proprietary infrastructure. **Goal:** Make biomedical research accessible, reproducible, and AI-augmented for every researcher, clinician, and developer — anywhere in the world. --- ## Why GenomeAI? | Problem | GenomeAI Solution | |---------|-------------------| | Biomedical data is scattered across 100+ databases | Unified connector layer — one API for all sources | | Existing tools require expensive licenses | 100% open-source, runs on free-tier APIs | | No integrated AI for genomic analysis | Multi-provider LLM support (Gemini cloud, Ollama local) | | Workflows are manual and error-prone | DAG-based workflow engine with retry, scheduling, and parallel execution | | Results are hard to visualize | Built-in genome browser, protein viewer, network graphs, scientific charts | | Reproducibility is difficult | Versioned workflows, provenance tracking, audit logs | --- ## Features ### Built and Working | Feature | Status | |---------|--------| | Biological domain models (Genome, Sample, Gene, Variant, Transcript, Protein, …) | ✅ | | REST API with CRUD + enhanced analysis endpoints (24 route modules) | ✅ | | Workflow DAG engine (definitions, steps, dependencies, validation) | ✅ | | Deterministic, parallel DAG execution | ✅ | | Cron-based workflow scheduler | ✅ | | Queue & worker (Redis-backed background execution) | ✅ | | Retry & failure handling (classification, backoff, policies) | ✅ | | 18 real external-data connectors (NCBI, UniProt, ClinVar, gnomAD, …) | ✅ | | AI-powered analysis (gene, variant, protein, drug, pathway, disease, literature, multi-domain report) with Gemini + Ollama | ✅ | | Genome browser, protein viewer, network graphs, scientific charts, molecular structure | ✅ | | Live demo — [genomeai.vercel.app](https://genomeai.vercel.app) | ✅ | ### Coming Next | Feature | Phase | |---------|-------| | Knowledge graph (gene-disease-drug-protein associations) | 5 | | More AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Mistral) | 6 | | PubMed/Europe PMC deep-dive literature QA | 6 | | Plugin SDK and marketplace | 7 | | Full-text ingestion workers (scheduled sync of source databases) | 7 | | Authentication & multi-user organizations | 8 | --- ## # ai-model-router

**OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway**: route every request to the *best, cheapest, or
fastest* model across providers, fall back automatically when a provider fails,
and see exactly what each call costs — all through an API your existing OpenAI
clients already speak.

v1.0.0 adds the production layer: **multi-tenant API keys, per-key rate limits,
persisted usage/billing, a semantic cache, guardrails, and an admin CLI** — so it
can run as a hosted subscription product, not just a local tool.

```sh
uv run ai-model-router db-init --db /var/lib/router/router.db
uv run ai-model-router create-key --db /var/lib/router/router.db --name my-app
# amr_live_<64 hex>  ->  keep this; it is shown once
ROUTER_DB=/var/lib/router/router.db \
ROUTER_API_KEY=admin-secret \
uv run ai-model-router serve
```

```python
# Point your existing OpenAI SDK at the router:
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="amr_live_...")
reply   = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="auto",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi"}],
    extra_body={"router": {"policy": "cheapest", "fallback": True}},
)
```

## Why

Companies spend far too much on LLMs because one model gets glued to one call
path. A router fixes three things at once:

- **Cost** — pick the cheapest model that can actually do the job
  (`gpt-4o-mini` instead of `gpt-4o` for a chat reply); repeat questions hit a
  **semantic cache** and cost zero.
- **Reliability** — when a provider returns 5xx / quota / timeout, fall through
  to the next model instead of failing the user's request.
- **Oversight** — per-request `estimated_cost_usd`, latency, persisted usage per
  API key, and a `/v1/usage` endpoint show your real spend across providers.

## Authentication & tiers

Every `amr_live_*` key is scoped to a rate-limit tier; limits are enforced
strictly (HTTP 429 with a reason when exceeded).

| Tier      | req/min | req/day | Intent |
|-----------|---------|---------|--------|
| `free`    | 30      | 500     | evaluate the gateway |
| `developer` | 60   | 5,000   | hobby / prototypes |
| `pro`     | 300     | 50,000  | production apps |
| `business`| 1,000   | 500,000 | teams |

`ROUTER_API_KEY` is an admin (unmetered) key. When no keys are configured the
gateway runs open and unmetered for local demos.

## How routing works

Constraint filtering happens first, then ordering by policy:

1. **Filter** by required capabilities (`tools`, `vision`, `json`,
   `long-context`), allowed providers, and an optional `max_cost_usd`.
2. **Order** by policy:
   - `priority` — your explicit model order (default: **measured** latency order)
   - `cheapest` — lowest list price (input + output)
   - `fastest` — lowest latency. Uses real measured averages from
     `ROUTER_DB` once telemetry exists, static hints before that.
3. **Try** the top candidate; on failure, move down the list until one succeeds
   (`fallback: true`, the default).

Set `"model": "auto"` for full automatic routing, or name a specific model to
start there and still fall back.

### Request-time routing hints

```jsonc
{
  "model": "auto",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this PDF page"}],
  "router": {
    "policy": "cheapest",
    "requires": ["vision"],
    "providers": ["openai", "anthropic", "google"],
    "max_cost_usd": 2.0,
    "priority": ["gpt-4o-mini", "claude-3-5-haiku", "gemini-2.0-flash"],
    "fallback": true,
    "cache_enabled": true,
    "redact_pii": false,
    "block_injection": false
  }
}
```

## Guardrails

Opt-in per request (and safe to leave on):

- **`redact_pii: true`** — replaces emails, phone numbers, SSN/card numbers and
  IPv4 addresses with `[REDACTED ...]` placeholders in the outbound prompt *and*
  the response, so PII never reaches a third-party provider.
- **`block_injection: true`** — rejects requests that look like prompt-injection
  attempts ("ignore your system prompt", "jailbreak", …) with a 400 before they
  are sent to any provider.

## Semantic cache

Enabled by default for text-only requests without tool calls; disable per request
with `"router": {"cache_enabled": false}`. Responses are keyed on a normalized
digest of the message history. A cached reply is served with
`route.router_reason = "semantic cache hit"`, `estimated_cost_usd = 0.0`, and is
recorded in usage as a cache hit.

## Endpoints

| Endpoint | Description |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | Routed chat. `stream: true` returns SSE. |
| `GET /v1/models` | Catalog of routable models. |
| `GET /v1/models/{id}` | Price / capabilities / latency for one model. |
| `GET /v1/usage` | Persisted spend, calls, cache hits, and avg latency per model. |
| `GET /v1/admin/health` | Provider + storage status (auth required). |
| `POST /webhooks/lemon` | Lemon Squeezy subscription webhook (see below). |
| `POST /signup` | Mint a free-tier API key (rate-limited per IP). |
| `GET /pricing`, `/` | Marketing landing page + tier prices. |
| `/health`, `/` | Liveness and endpoint summary. Interactive docs at `/docs`. |

Every response includes a `route` block:

```json
{
  "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 18, "completion_tokens": 24, "total_tokens": 42,
             "estimated_cost_usd": 0.000017},
  "route": {
    "requested_model": "auto", "chosen_model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "provider": "openai", "policy_used": "cheapest",
    "attempts": 2, "fallback_used": true,
    "latency_ms": 431, "estimated_cost_usd": 0.000017,
    "router_reason": "served by openai after 1 failure(s)"
  }
}
```

## Admin CLI

```sh
ai-model-router db-init --db router.db        # create schema
ai-model-router create-key --db router.db --name api --tier pro
ai-model-router list-keys --db router.db      # prefix + tier only
ai-model-router revoke-key --db router.db 3
ai-model-router usage --db router.db
```

## Billing (Lemon Squeezy)

Create product variants whose names contain `developer`, `pro`, or `business`,
and pass the API key id through `custom_data.key_id` at checkout. Point the store
webhook at `POST /webhooks/lemon` and set `LEMON_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Purchases
upgrade the key's tier; cancellation/expiry downgrade it to `free`.

## Providers

| Variable | Provider | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | openai | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` to override |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | anthropic | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to override |
| `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | google | `GOOGLE_BASE_URL` to override |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | openrouter | any OpenAI-compatible model via OpenRouter |
| — | mock | always enabled; `ROUTER_MOCK_FAIL_MODELS` forces failures for tests |

## Deploy

The repo ships `Dockerfile` (non-root + healthcheck), `fly.toml`
(Fly.io + persistent disk), and `render.yaml` (Render blueprint). Deploy docs:
[docs/deploy.md](docs/deploy.md). Container images are published to
`ghcr.io/dsk-dev-ai/ai-model-router` and the Python package
`pip install ai-model-router-gateway` on tagged releases.

## Docs

- [docs/quickstart.md](docs/quickstart.md) — 5-minute setup guide
- [docs/deploy.md](docs/deploy.md) — Fly.io / Render / Docker deployments
- [docs/admin.md](docs/admin.md) — key management & usage
- [docs/billing.md](docs/billing.md) — Lemon Squeezy integration
- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) — design notes
- [docs/api.md](docs/api.md) — API reference

## Install & run

```sh
uv sync --group dev
uv run pytest -q
uv run mypy -p ai_model_router
uv run ruff check src tests
uv run ai-model-router serve
```

Try it:

```sh
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer amr_live_...' \
  -d '{"model":"auto","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}],
       "router":{"policy":"cheapest"}}'
```

## Provider Manager

The Provider Manager is implemented in ``packages/llm/`` and provides:

- **``LLMProvider`` interface** — 6 methods: ``chat``, ``chat_stream``, ``embed``, ``embed_stream``, ``health``, ``list_models``
- **``ProviderRegistry``** — Register, get, list, unregister providers by name
- **``ModelRouter``** — Capability-based routing: primary → fallback → error
- **``CircuitBreaker``** — Opens after N consecutive failures, cooldown then half-open
- **``HealthChecker``** — Periodic health probes with TTL cache
- **``TokenBucketRateLimiter``** — Smooths request rates per provider
- **``RetryPolicy``** — Exponential backoff with ±25% jitter
- **Providers** — NVIDIA NIM adapter (primary), Ollama adapter (fallback)

```python
from bookforge.llm import ProviderManager
from bookforge.llm.models import Message, MessageRole

manager = ProviderManager.from_env()
await manager.start()
response = await manager.chat([
    Message(role=MessageRole.USER, content="Write a chapter...")
])
await manager.stop()
```

# BUG DROP — The Superpower Vending Machine

[![CI](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/bugdrop-portfolio/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/bugdrop-portfolio/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE)

A personal portfolio for the **AWS Student Builder Challenge: Build Your Tech Superpower**.
Instead of listing skills, BUG DROP dispenses the **superpowers I earned from real bugs**:
every capsule opens as an incident postmortem (incident → root cause → fix → lesson → the
project it made possible).

- **Live site:** https://main.d37v5f104dujlp.amplifyapp.com
- **Repo:** `https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/bugdrop-portfolio`
- **Built with:** HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript
- **Hosted on:** AWS Amplify Hosting (+ optional API Gateway / Lambda / DynamoDB counter)

![BUG DROP architecture](docs/architecture.svg)

## The creative feature

![BUG DROP feature flow](docs/feature-flow.svg)

1. A blinking **"PULL FOR A SUPERPOWER"** hint points at the lever.
2. Pulling the lever shakes the machine and drops a capsule.
3. The capsule opens an **incident postmortem** card with a real bug, its root cause,
   the fix, the lesson, and the project that came out of it.
4. The **third pull unlocks a secret capsule**.
5. Opened capsules are saved to a **capsule cabinet** with a progress bar, so the
   collection can be revisited later.
6. An **unlocked profile** turns the collection into domain bars (Debugging, APIs,
   Data, Deploy, Frontend, Security, Accessibility, Mindset) as capsules open.
7. Every postmortem has a **shareable deep link** (`#capsule=c03`) and a copy-link
   button; the cabinet can open a capsule without pulling again.
8. **Export unlocked** downloads the opened postmortems as Markdown, and **Reset
   local progress** replays the machine without touching the AWS counter.
9. The lever is a real `<button>` and works with mouse, touch, keyboard, and screen readers.
10. No camera, no permissions, no external API keys — the feature works even if the
    network API is down.

## Core portfolio sections

- **About Me** — who I am and how I learn.
- **Skills / Tech Superpowers** — powers framed as things earned, not just listed.
- **Projects / Achievements** — projects with the bug stories behind them.
- **Under the hood** — a visible AWS architecture diagram, the service map, and
  links to the SAM template and deploy runbook.

## Project structure

```text
bugdrop-portfolio/
├─ index.html                 # single-page portfolio
├─ 404.html                   # branded not-found page
├─ manifest.webmanifest       # installable web app metadata
├─ assets/
│  ├─ css/style.css           # theme + responsive layout + animations
│  ├─ js/config.js            # API base URL + GitHub link (edit this)
│  ├─ js/core.js              # pure helpers: deep links, cabinet, progress
│  ├─ js/machine.js           # vending machine + postmortem modal
│  ├─ js/app.js               # navigation
│  ├─ js/capsules.json        # ← your bug stories live here
│  └─ img/
│     ├─ og-cover.png         # 1200x675 social cover (generated)
│     ├─ og-cover.svg         # editable source for the cover
│     ├─ icon.svg             # vector app icon
│     └─ icon-512.png         # maskable app icon
├─ backend/
│  ├─ template.yaml           # AWS SAM: HTTP API + Lambda + DynamoDB
│  └─ src/
│     ├─ handler.mjs          # /pull /stats /daily
│     ├─ lib.mjs              # pure helpers (routing, day-of-year, daily pick)
│     └─ capsules.json        # mirror used by /daily

│  ├─ architecture.svg        # architecture diagram for the submission

```

## 1. Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm run serve      # http://localhost:8080
```

Or with no dependencies:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

> Open it through a server, not `file://`, so `capsules.json` can be fetched.

## 2. Make it yours

Edit **`assets/js/capsules.json`**:

```json

  "capsules": [
    {
      "id": "c01",
      "superpower": "The 2AM Debugger",
      "bug": "What actually broke.",
      "cause": "Why it broke.",
      "fix": "How you fixed it.",
      "lesson": "What you now always do.",
      "project": "What it helped you build.",
      "domain": "Debugging",
      "evidence": "commit / screenshot / link"
    }
  ],
  "secret": { "id": "secret", "superpower": "...", "bug": "...", "cause": "...", "fix": "...", "lesson": "...", "project": "...", "evidence": "..." }

```

## 3. Deploy to AWS Amplify Hosting (required)

The full checklist, verification steps, and troubleshooting live in
**[`docs/DEPLOY.md`](docs/DEPLOY.md)**.

1. Push this folder to a **public** GitHub repository.
2. AWS Console → **Amplify** → **Create new app** → **Host web app**.
3. Connect GitHub → choose the repo and the `main` branch.
4. Amplify reads `amplify.yml` automatically → **Save and deploy**.
5. Copy the live URL (`https://main.xxxxxxxx.amplifyapp.com`).
6. Amplify serves the branded `404.html` for unknown paths; no rewrite is needed
   for this single-page static site.
7. Optional: **App settings → Previews** to build pull requests, and **Domain management**
   for a custom domain.

Keep the app running through **November 23** (judging window).

## 4. Optional AWS serverless counter

Adds a real serverless backend to the creative feature: a global "capsules pulled"
counter and a daily superpower.

> **Managed Builder Center projects:** the “Future Unicorn” project uses a
> Service Control Policy that denies CloudFormation, Lambda, API Gateway, and
> DynamoDB creation. SAM cannot deploy there. Submit the Amplify-only site; the
> counter is optional. Deploy this backend only from a standalone AWS account.

```bash
cd backend
sam build
sam deploy --guided
# Stack name: bugdrop-api
# AllowedOrigin: https://main.xxxxxxxx.amplifyapp.com
```

Then copy the **ApiBaseUrl** output into `assets/js/config.js`:

```js
window.BUGDROP_CONFIG = {
  apiBase: "https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com",
  github: "https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai"
};
```

Push again; Amplify redeploys. The machine calls:

| Method | Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/pull` | Atomically increments the global counter |
| `GET` | `/stats` | Reads the global counter |
| `GET` | `/daily` | Returns a deterministic "superpower of the day" |

creative feature never breaks.

### AWS services used (for the write-up)

**Live:**
- **AWS Amplify Hosting** — build + deploy from GitHub, HTTPS, live URL.
- **Amazon CloudFront** — global CDN delivered by Amplify.

- **Amazon DynamoDB** — `capsule_stats` table, atomic counter item.
- **AWS IAM** — least-privilege role generated by SAM.
- **Amazon CloudWatch** — Lambda logs.

## 5. CI/CD

- **Continuous deployment:** every push to `main` triggers an Amplify build and deploy.
- **Pull request previews:** enable in Amplify → Previews.
- **GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`):**

  - Stylelint — CSS
  - Linkinator — broken local links
  - Lighthouse CI — performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO

Run locally:

```bash
npm run lint
npm test
npm run serve
npm run links
npm run lighthouse
```

## 6. Tests

The test suite runs on Node's built-in test runner (no extra dependencies):

```bash
npm test
```

It checks:

- the capsule dataset schema, unique ids, and the secret capsule (`tests/capsules.test.mjs`)

Fill the Builder Center **Create a project** form using `docs/SUBMISSION.md`.

ErasureProof is a deletion-audit and remediation engine. It reconstructs a person's identity from current and historical identifiers, finds their records across databases, replicas, search indexes, analytics, support systems, logs, exports, archives and backups, applies your erasure policy, remediates in a safe dependency order, verifies the result, and issues a signed, tamper-evident attestation. Deletion workflows usually report success because the primary database deleted a row. ErasureProof treats those statuses as claims. It proves the state of every copy at a point in time — including active sync jobs and restorable backups that can recreate data after deletion. ## Why this exists - **Ghost data is normal.** Replicas, search indexes, analytics pipelines, exports, support attachments and backups retain identifiers long after the source row is gone. - **Workflow status is not evidence.** A `COMPLETE` badge does not prove that a person's data is absent or that retained records were properly redacted. - **Regulators want proof.** A deletion request needs a defensible record of what was found, what was changed, what was deliberately retained, and how the final state was verified. ## How it works ```text Request ──► Intent classifier ──► Identity graph (current + historical IDs) │ ▼ Connector fan-out (read-only discovery) │ ▼ Policy engine ──► Findings + ordered remediation plan │ ▼ Flow/restore controls ──► Record remediation │ ▼ Re-discovery ──► Verification ──► Signed attestation + hash-chained ledger ``` 1. **Intent.** Only an explicit, non-negated deletion request authorizes action. Access, correction, export, marketing opt-out and restriction requests are reported as `NOT_APPLICABLE`. 2. **Identity.** Current and historical emails, phones and email hashes are reunited into one subject graph, so old identifiers still found in logs and analytics are in scope. 3. **Discovery.** Connectors enumerate matching records, active data flows and restore points. The filesystem connector extracts PDF text, image OCR, Office/archive members, SQLite snapshots, EXIF and printable strings, so a match does not depend on a filename. Each snapshot is written to a content-addressed evidence store. 4. **Policy.** A YAML policy maps each category to `DELETE`, `REDACT`, `ANONYMIZE`, `RETAIN` or `TOMBSTONE`. Legal holds and retention obligations override erasure. 5. **Planning.** Findings cite evidence. Remediation disables flows and blocks restores first, then removes downstream copies before their source records. A dependency graph validates the order and exposes a critical path. 6. **Verification.** The engine re-discovers state after remediation and checks every expected outcome; it does not trust action success flags. 7. **Attestation.** The outcome, plan and verification results are canonicalised, signed with HMAC-SHA256 and committed to a SHA-256 hash-chained ledger. ## What ships in 1.1 | Prove the state | Remediate safely | Operate with confidence | | --- | --- | --- | | Identity graph over current and historical identifiers | Policy engine for delete, redact, anonymize, retain, and tombstone | API-key or OIDC auth with tenant isolation and roles | | Evidence extraction for PDF, OCR, Office, archives, SQLite, logs, and images | Dependency-ordered plan that controls flows and restores first | Approval-gated destructive runs with separation of duties | | Signed HMAC attestations plus a hash-chained ledger | Re-discovery and verification that never trusts action flags | Audit events, CSV export, signed backups, metrics, and probes | | Interactive remediation DAG in JSON, Mermaid, or DOT | Built-in SQL, object-store, filesystem, S3, and control connectors | Hosted console, Python SDK, Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes | - **Authentication and tenant isolation** with static API keys or OIDC, viewer/operator/administrator roles, and server-side tenant scoping. - **Self-service onboarding** with isolated sandboxes, seeded connectors, one-time keys, per-IP quotas, and expiry. - **Approval-gated remediation** where a second administrator authorizes a single-use, time-limited destructive run. - **Tamper-evident auditing** with tenant-scoped CSV export and signed backups of evidence, the ledger, attestations, and metadata. - **A hardened edge** with request IDs, per-IP rate limiting, Prometheus metrics, security headers, configurable CORS, readiness probes, and Kubernetes manifests. - **A full console** for overview metrics, request audits, identity graphs, remediation plans, evidence inspection, ledger verification, policy review, API keys, and demo discovery. - **Evidence intelligence** for PDFs, images, OCR, Office files, archives, SQLite snapshots, metadata, and free text. - **Authorized exposure discovery** for public URLs, web archives, search APIs, breach metadata, and public profiles — passive checks only, disabled by default. - **A step dependency graph** that validates ordering and renders as Mermaid, Graphviz DOT, JSON, or an interactive console view. ## Install ```bash pip install erasureproof ``` Install database, OIDC, object-store, or workflow extras as needed: ```bash pip install "erasureproof[postgres]" pip install "erasureproof[oidc]" pip install "erasureproof[s3]" pip install "erasureproof[temporal]" ``` The core CLI is on [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/erasureproof/). The standalone Python client is published separately as [`erasureproof-sdk`](https://pypi.org/project/erasureproof-sdk/): ```bash pip install erasureproof-sdk ``` ## Quickstart For local development from source, use Python 3.10+ (3.11/3.12 recommended) and `uv` or `pip`: ```bash # with uv (recommended) uv venv .venv uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e ".[dev]" # or with a standard virtualenv python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate pip install -e ".[dev]" ``` Once installed from PyPI, run the demo directly with `erasureproof demo` or `uvx erasureproof demo`. ### Run the end-to-end demo ```bash .venv/bin/erasureproof demo ``` The demo seeds a fictional commerce platform (SQLite + local object bucket + control plane), runs a GDPR erasure for `alice@example.com`, remediates every copy, verifies the result and writes a signed attestation under `.erasureproof/attestations/`. Expected output ends with `status: COMPLETE` and all verification checks passing. Useful follow-ups: ```bash .venv/bin/erasureproof demo --json .venv/bin/erasureproof demo --graph # Mermaid step DAG .venv/bin/erasureproof ledger verify .venv/bin/erasureproof attestation verify .erasureproof/attestations/.attestation.json # Scan an export directory for current or historical identifiers. .venv/bin/erasureproof scan ./exports --email alice@example.com --name "Alice Example" # Render a stored plan/result as a graph. .venv/bin/erasureproof graph result.json --format dot ``` ### Run the API ```bash .venv/bin/erasureproof serve --reload # OpenAPI docs: http://localhost:8000/docs ``` Local development defaults to `ERASUREPROOF_AUTH_MODE=disabled`. Production startup fails unless authentication is enabled and the attestation key is changed. For a static-key deployment: ```bash export ERASUREPROOF_ENVIRONMENT=production export ERASUREPROOF_AUTH_MODE=api_key export ERASUREPROOF_ATTESTATION_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" export ERASUREPROOF_API_KEYS='[{"key":"replace-me","role":"admin","tenant_id":"*","subject":"admin"}]' export ERASUREPROOF_REQUIRE_REMEDIATION_APPROVAL=true export ERASUREPROOF_CORS_ORIGINS=https://erasureproof.example.com ``` Send the key as `Authorization: Bearer ` or `X-API-Key: `. OIDC mode validates RS256/384/512 tokens against the configured issuer, audience, and JWKS URL; install the `oidc` extra. ### Run the web console The console is a Vite + React application in `web/`. It ships a landing page, an operations dashboard, request audits, a remediation dependency graph, identity and connector views, evidence/ledger inspection, passive exposure scanning, policy configuration, and built-in product documentation. The console is a private npm workspace (`"private": true`) and is not published to npm; it is built into the Python deployment image. Install the console dependencies once, then run both processes from the repository root: ```bash npm install --prefix web npm run dev # Console: http://localhost:5173 # API: http://localhost:8000 ``` `npm run dev` starts the FastAPI API (with reload) and the Vite console together. Use `npm run dev:api` or `npm run dev:web` to start only one side. The root scripts require an existing `.venv` created during installation. For a production build served by FastAPI: ```bash npm run build .venv/bin/erasureproof serve # Console: http://localhost:8000/console ``` The Vite build requires Node 22 or newer and uses `/console/` as its production base. FastAPI serves hashed assets with immutable caching and falls back to `index.html` for client routes. Seed the non-destructive demo workspace from the landing page or with: ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/demo/seed ``` When authentication is enabled, open the key button in the console top bar (or Settings → API access) and paste a bearer token. Evidence downloads use the same authenticated request, so private artifacts never require a public URL. ### Hosted demo and developer API The hosted demo runs at : the console is at `/console`, OpenAPI at `/docs`, and the API under `/v1`. Create a free isolated sandbox with a one-time API key: ```bash curl -s -X POST "$BASE_URL/v1/onboarding/sandbox" \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"workspace_name":"Acme privacy"}' ``` Use the returned key with the Python SDK: ```python from erasureproof_sdk import create_sandbox client, sandbox = create_sandbox("https://erasureproof.onrender.com") run = client.run_request(sandbox["sample_request_id"], remediate=False) print(run["status"], run["attestation"]["signature"]) ``` See [`docs/API.md`](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/erasureproof/blob/main/docs/API.md) for endpoint, role, approval, and error reference, and [`docs/DEPLOY_RENDER.md`](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/erasureproof/blob/main/docs/DEPLOY_RENDER.md) for the Render deployment profile. > [!WARNING] > The hosted instance is an evaluation sandbox, not durable evidence storage. > Render's free web filesystem is ephemeral, so evidence, ledger, attestation, > and sandbox-connector files are lost on restart, deploy, or host migration. > The hosted database is Neon Free in AWS US West (Oregon), with no 30-day > database expiry. Neon's free compute, storage, and egress limits apply. The > legacy Render Postgres was deleted after the migration was verified. For > durable evidence, attach a persistent disk or shared volume. ErasureProof's > evidence store is filesystem-backed; an object-store backend is not built in. ### Docker ```bash docker compose up --build # Console: http://localhost:8000/console # API: http://localhost:8000 # Docs: http://localhost:8000/docs ``` That compose file is a local demo with authentication disabled. For a hardened single-host deployment with an external PostgreSQL database, API-key auth, required approvals, metrics token, and HSTS: ```bash export ERASUREPROOF_DATABASE_URL='postgresql+psycopg://...' export ERASUREPROOF_ATTESTATION_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" export ERASUREPROOF_API_KEYS='[{"key":"...","role":"admin","tenant_id":"*","subject":"admin"}]' export ERASUREPROOF_METRICS_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" export ERASUREPROOF_CORS_ORIGINS='https://erasureproof.example.com' docker compose -f docker-compose.production.yml up -d --build ``` The image uses a multi-stage build: Node builds the console, then the Python runtime bundles the static assets with OCR and document tooling. Create a tenant, register connectors, submit a request and run it: ```bash curl -s localhost:8000/v1/tenants \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"name":"Acme","jurisdiction":"gdpr"}' curl -s localhost:8000/v1/requests \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"tenant_id":"","email":"alice@example.com","request_text":"Please delete my account.","audit_at":"2026-10-26T00:00:00Z"}' curl -s -X POST 'localhost:8000/v1/requests//run?remediate=true' curl -s localhost:8000/v1/requests//attestation ``` ## Connector SDK Connectors are the only components that touch customer systems. Implement the methods you need: ```python from erasureproof.connectors.base import BaseConnector class MyWarehouseConnector(BaseConnector): type = "warehouse" def discover(self, subject, as_of): # return list[ResourceRef] for matching records ... def remediate(self, ref, action, fields=()): # delete/redact/anonymize the record ... def discover_flows(self, subject, as_of): # return list[FlowRef] for active sync/import jobs ... def discover_backups(self, subject, as_of): # return list[BackupRef] for restorable snapshots ... ``` Built-in connectors: | Type | Purpose | |---|---| | `sql` | SQLite, Postgres, MySQL and any SQLAlchemy URL | | `postgres` | Postgres-aware SQL connector | | `local` | Local object-store directory (exports, attachments, logs) | | `filesystem` / `workspace` | Directory tree with PDF/OCR/archive/SQLite extraction and redaction | | `s3` | S3-compatible bucket (`pip install "erasureproof[s3]"`) | | `control` | JSON control plane for sync jobs and backup restore points | Connector configs are stored per tenant in the API and are validated before use. SQL table and column names are allow-listed; values are always bound parameters. ## Policy Policies live in `policies/*.yaml`: ```yaml name: GDPR Erasure Policy jurisdiction: gdpr defaults: PRIMARY_ACCOUNT: action: TOMBSTONE redact_fields: [name, email, phone, email_hash] retain_fields: [user_id] rules: - name: legal-hold-retained priority: 100 when: {payload.legal_hold: true} action: RETAIN ``` Actions: | Action | Effect | |---|---| | `DELETE` | Remove the whole record | | `REDACT` | Keep the record, remove required direct identifiers | | `ANONYMIZE` | Keep the record, irreversibly unlink it from the subject | | `RETAIN` | Keep the record (legal hold, audit, statutory retention) | | `TOMBSTONE` | Keep the stable subject reference, remove direct identifiers | ## Evidence intelligence The `intelligence` package is intentionally local and deterministic: | Input | What is extracted | |---|---| | Text, JSON, CSV, HTML, XML, logs | Full text plus bounded context snippets | | PDF | Embedded text; page OCR fallback via `pdftoppm` + `tesseract` | | Images | OCR text and EXIF metadata (GPS fields are not copied into findings) | | DOCX/XLSX/PPTX | Office XML text, comments and document metadata | | ZIP/TAR/GZ | Bounded member extraction, recursion depth and size caps | | SQLite | Table names, schema and text columns, bounded row sampling | | Unknown binaries | Printable strings fallback, marked low confidence | Matches are mapped to normalized emails, phones, email hashes, handles, URLs, IPs and other identifiers. Output is masked by default; raw evidence stays in the content-addressed store and is referenced by `evidence_id`. Scanned trees are read-only and symlinks are never followed. `scan` writes evidence under `.erasureproof/evidence/`, enforces a file limit, and never writes into the scanned directory. OCR requires `tesseract` and `pdftoppm` on `PATH`; PDF text extraction works without them. ## Authorized exposure discovery Exposure checks are **off by default** and require explicit per-scan approval. They are passive: ErasureProof reads public sources, never bypasses authentication, never exploits a target and never downloads breach dumps. ```bash export ERASUREPROOF_EXPOSURE_ENABLED=true .venv/bin/erasureproof exposure \ --email alice@example.com \ --url https://example.com/team \ --authorized ``` Collectors: | Collector | What it checks | |---|---| | `direct` | Operator-supplied public URLs | | `wayback` | Internet Archive CDX snapshots for supplied URLs | | `search` | Serper or Brave search APIs for quoted identifiers | | `hibp` | Have I Been Pwned breach metadata (no passwords) | | `github` | GitHub code search using a token | | `gravatar` | Public Gravatar profile for an email hash | | `username` | Public GitHub/Keybase account existence | Guardrails: scheme and credential rejection, private/link-local/loopback DNS blocking, redirect re-validation, robots.txt enforcement for page fetches, per-host rate limits, response-size and timeout caps, and collector isolation. Search and breach collectors require their own API keys and provider terms. Results are masked in the report and the raw response is stored as evidence. The `--authorized` flag is an operator assertion, not user authentication. Put the API behind your own authentication and authorization layer before enabling exposure scanning, and only check identifiers you are entitled to investigate. ## Step graph The planner emits a safe order; the graph proves and visualises it. Findings are roots, flow/restore controls precede record changes, downstream copies precede primary accounts, and each verification depends on the action that produced its state. ```bash curl -s localhost:8000/v1/requests//graph curl -s 'localhost:8000/v1/requests//graph?format=mermaid' curl -s 'localhost:8000/v1/requests//graph?format=dot' ``` The API `run` response, attestation payload and `demo --graph` include the same DAG. Nodes carry phase, operation, state, system/resource and dependencies. ## Approvals, audit and backup When `ERASUREPROOF_REQUIRE_REMEDIATION_APPROVAL=true`, a request creator cannot run destructive remediation until a **different administrator** approves it. Approvals are single-use, expire after `ERASUREPROOF_APPROVAL_TTL_HOURS`, and are consumed atomically before the run. Audit-only runs (`?remediate=false`) do not require approval. Administrative events (request creation, runs, approvals, tenant and connector changes, exposure scans) are written to `audit_events` and exposed as tenant-scoped JSON and CSV: ```bash curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ 'localhost:8000/v1/audit-events?limit=100' curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -o audit.csv 'localhost:8000/v1/audit-events/export' ``` Create and verify a signed backup archive: ```bash .venv/bin/erasureproof backup create --output /secure/backups/erasureproof.zip .venv/bin/erasureproof backup verify /secure/backups/erasureproof.zip ``` The archive contains evidence objects, the ledger, attestations, and a SQLite snapshot when the metadata store is SQLite. It is signed with the attestation key; a wrong key or modified member fails verification. Back up PostgreSQL separately with your provider's tooling. Restoring refuses to overwrite live data unless `--force` is supplied and the destination is outside the live data directories. ## Evidence, ledger and attestations - **Evidence store** (`evidence/store.py`) writes immutable snapshots under their SHA-256. Identical content is stored once. - **Ledger** (`evidence/ledger.py`) is append-only JSONL where each entry commits to the previous hash. `erasureproof ledger verify` detects edits, deletions and reordering. - **Attestation** (`core/attestation.py`) is a canonical JSON document containing the status, ordered plan, verification results and ledger head, signed with HMAC-SHA256. Replace `ERASUREPROOF_ATTESTATION_KEY` with a KMS/Vault-backed signer in production. ## Configuration Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and adjust: ```text ERASUREPROOF_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///./.erasureproof/erasureproof.db ERASUREPROOF_DATA_DIR=./.erasureproof ERASUREPROOF_WEB_DIR=./web/dist ERASUREPROOF_DEMO_ENABLED=true ERASUREPROOF_SELF_SERVE_ENABLED=false ERASUREPROOF_SANDBOX_TTL_HOURS=168 ERASUREPROOF_ATTESTATION_KEY=change-me ERASUREPROOF_POLICY_DIR=./policies ERASUREPROOF_DEFAULT_JURISDICTION=gdpr # Production access control. Production refuses auth_mode=disabled. ERASUREPROOF_AUTH_MODE=disabled # ERASUREPROOF_API_KEYS=[{"key":"...","role":"admin","tenant_id":"*","subject":"admin"}] # ERASUREPROOF_OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.com # ERASUREPROOF_OIDC_AUDIENCE=erasureproof # ERASUREPROOF_OIDC_JWKS_URL=https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json ERASUREPROOF_REQUIRE_REMEDIATION_APPROVAL=false ERASUREPROOF_APPROVAL_TTL_HOURS=24 # Edge and observability. Put TLS and rate limits at the gateway too. ERASUREPROOF_CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://127.0.0.1:5173 ERASUREPROOF_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=0 ERASUREPROOF_HSTS_SECONDS=0 # ERASUREPROOF_METRICS_TOKEN= # Passive exposure discovery is opt-in. Keep the API key values in a secret store. ERASUREPROOF_EXPOSURE_ENABLED=false # ERASUREPROOF_SERPER_API_KEY= # ERASUREPROOF_BRAVE_API_KEY= # ERASUREPROOF_GITHUB_TOKEN= # ERASUREPROOF_HIBP_API_KEY= ``` SQLite is the default so the demo needs no external services. Set a `postgresql+psycopg://` URL and install the `postgres` extra for production. ## Development ```bash make check # ruff + pytest + console typecheck/build ``` The test suite covers intent classification, identity resolution, policy decisions, DAG ordering, evidence extraction (text/JSON/PDF/ZIP), workspace scanning, filesystem redaction, exposure authorization/scoring with fake HTTP, SQL/object-store remediation, ledger tamper detection, attestation signature verification, the API and the full demo. OCR tests are skipped when host OCR tools are unavailable. ## Web console The console reads the same REST API as the CLI.

Overview: proven findings, verification rate, attestation coverage, risk, evidence, and the live ledger. Open full size.

It contains: | View | Purpose | |---|---| | Landing | Product overview and one-click demo bootstrap. | | Overview | Status mix, audit trend, verification rate, risk, recent audits, and live ledger. | | Requests | Search, filters, intent state, and audit cutoff. | | Request detail | Findings, remediation plan, dependency graph, evidence, verification, and signed attestation. | | Subjects | Current and historical identifiers resolved into stable subjects. | | Connectors | Source inventory and connection configuration. | | Exposure | Authorized passive scan of public sources with safety guardrails. | | Evidence & ledger | Artifact integrity checks, hash-chain verification, and the policy matrix. | | Settings | Theme, workspace, bearer token, audit export, runtime, and environment configuration. | | API keys | Create, rotate, revoke, and audit tenant-scoped keys. | | Docs | Product, architecture, API, deployment, and security documentation. | Animation is implemented with Framer Motion, charts with Recharts, and server state with TanStack Query. The UI respects `prefers-reduced-motion` and includes a keyboard command palette (`Cmd/Ctrl+K`). ## Changelog See [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md) for release history. ## Design decisions - **Evidence before action.** Discovery snapshots are written before remediation, so the finding is reproducible even after the record is gone. - **Planner is deterministic.** Phase order is fixed; resources are ordered by dependency rank, then system ID and resource ID. - **Connectors are narrow.** They expose discovery, remediation and flow/restore control — no policy or identity logic — which keeps customer credentials and data-access code isolated. - **In-process by default.** Temporal is optional; the orchestrator is a plain function so it can be scheduled by any durable workflow engine. - **No silent trust.** Verification re-reads state instead of trusting delete return codes, and attestations commit to the verification results. ## Roadmap - Durable Temporal workflows backed by the approval ledger - Residency-aware multi-region connectors and retention calendars - Per-connector OAuth/KMS credential management - Continuous resurrection monitoring (alert when deleted data reappears) - Scheduled exposure rescans with diffing and archive/cache takedown tracking - Attestation transparency log and third-party verifier CLI - Policy simulation and dry-run impact reports ## Kubernetes Production manifests live in [`deploy/kubernetes`](deploy/kubernetes). They run two or more replicas against managed PostgreSQL and a shared `ReadWriteMany` volume, enable API-key authentication, require remediation approval, add probes, HPA, ingress TLS, and a default-deny network policy. See the deployment README before applying. ## Security Never commit credentials. Connector secrets should come from a secret manager or environment variables. In production, startup validation rejects disabled authentication and the default attestation key. Use one API key per operator, scope keys to a tenant, keep a wildcard admin key offline, and scrape `/metrics` with a dedicated token. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for reporting guidance and [`deploy/kubernetes`](deploy/kubernetes) for hardening notes. ## Release verification [`v1.1.2`](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/erasureproof/releases/tag/v1.1.2) is the current stable release. It hardens deletion-status decisions, evidence isolation, path handling, and cross-process mutation safety. The release gate is: ```bash make check # ruff, pytest, console typecheck and production build make package-check # both sdists/wheels plus twine metadata docker build -t erasureproof . docker run --rm -p 18000:8000 erasureproof curl -fsS localhost:18000/healthz ``` CI runs lint, the full test suite, package metadata checks, and the production console build on every push, pull request, and release tag. The hosted deployment is smoke-tested for health, readiness, sandbox creation, audit execution, attestation verification, and ledger integrity. See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for the release history and [docs/RELEASE.md](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/erasureproof/blob/main/docs/RELEASE.md) for the release evidence. ## Sponsor ErasureProof If ErasureProof saves you time, you can support continued development through [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/dsk-dev-ai). Sponsorship funds connector coverage, regression tests, and hosted demo infrastructure.

# HackerRank Orchestrate - October 2026

## Ghost Data Still Exists

Build an AI agent that audits whether a user's personal data was actually deleted.

A deletion workflow may report **Complete** while data still exists in databases, logs, support attachments, exports, search indexes, archives, or backups. Sync and restore processes may also bring deleted data back.

For each request, the agent must first determine whether deletion was actually requested. It then returns `COMPLETE`, `INCOMPLETE`, or `NOT_APPLICABLE`, reports any remaining data or recreation risk, and produces the ordered remediation and verification steps required to finish an authorized deletion safely.

Read [`problem_statement.md`](./problem_statement.md) for the complete challenge contract.

## Live Demo

**Live demo:** https://ghost-data-still-exists-demo.onrender.com (Gemini explanations enabled)

The demo is deployed on Render's free tier from
[`dsk-dev-ai/ghost-data-still-exists`](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/ghost-data-still-exists)
using [`render.yaml`](./render.yaml). It browses all 518 cases, shows findings and
remediation steps, and can explain any case with Gemini when `GEMINI_API_KEY` is
configured. See [`README_DEMO.md`](./README_DEMO.md) for local and Render setup.

---

## Quick Start

Clone the repository and move into the project directory:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/interviewstreet/hackerrank-orchestrate-october26.git
cd hackerrank-orchestrate-october26
```

Start your AI coding tool from the **repository root** so it automatically reads [`AGENTS.md`](./AGENTS.md) and logs your session turns to `log.txt` in the root directory.

Build your solution in `code/main.py`, or use another language and document its setup and run command clearly in your README.

Your solution must:

- Read the input files from `dataset/`
- Generate one prediction row for every request in `dataset/deletion_requests.csv`
- Write the final predictions to `output.csv` in the repository root

Run the starter Python entry point with:

```bash
python3 code/main.py
```

The blank template at `dataset/output.csv` is provided as a reference. Your final generated file for submission must be the root-level `output.csv`.


## Dataset

All participant-facing files are in `dataset/`:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `deletion_requests.csv` | 518 requests |
| `sample_deletion_requests.csv` | 32 sample requests |
| `sample_output.csv` | Correct sample answers |
| `user_identities.csv` | Current user identities |
| `user_audit_log.csv` | Historical identity changes |
| `system_activity.csv` | Activity across services and data processes |
| `deletion_rules.csv` | Required treatment for each data category |
| `evidence_files.csv` | Manifest of supplied evidence files |
| `output.csv` | Blank output template |

Evidence is stored under `dataset/evidence/` and may include PDFs, images, logs, JSON, plain text, or SQL snapshot exports. SQL captures may contain a primary database, regional replicas, a reporting replica, or a failover replica so replication drift can be investigated directly. The `.sql` files are readable as text and executable with SQLite.

Only `deletion_requests.csv` requires answers. The other files provide evidence and context.

---

## Output

Create `output.csv` with these columns in this exact order:

```text
case_id,deletion_status,steps_json
```

Produce exactly one row per request. `deletion_status` is `COMPLETE`, `INCOMPLETE`, or `NOT_APPLICABLE`. `steps_json` is an ordered JSON array containing findings, remediation actions, and verification checks. Use an empty array (`[]`) for `NOT_APPLICABLE`. Evidence references may be a `file_id`, `activity_id`, or `audit_id`. Determine the resource state at `audit_at` from the available evidence; reported workflow statuses and operation results are claims. Use `dataset/sample_output.csv` as the format reference.

The final file must contain 518 data rows sorted by `case_id` (plus the header row). The grader parses `steps_json` as JSON, so object-key order and whitespace do not matter; array order does. Order findings, remediation, and verification in that phase order. Within a phase, follow the operation order in the problem statement, then sort by `system_id` and `resource_id`.

---

## Evaluation

`output.csv` will be compared with hidden canonical answers. Scoring considers:

- deletion assessment accuracy;
- current and historical identity resolution;
- discovery of remaining data and recreation risks;
- correct policy application and evidence references; and
- completeness and ordering of remediation and verification steps.

Your `code.zip` must include:


| --- | --- |

---

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `code.zip` | Runnable solution, prompts, configuration, `README.md`, and `evaluation/` reports |

# DistrLab **Break a live distributed system — right in your browser.** Simulate cache stampedes, queue backpressure, rate limiting, load-balancing strategies, network partitions and replica lag in real time. Flip the switches, watch latency, throughput, errors and queue depth react — then read the plain-language explanation of *why*. [Try it live](https://distrlab.onrender.com) · [Releases](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/distrlab/releases) · [Report a bug](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai/distrlab/issues) ![live](https://img.shields.io/website?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdistrlab.onrender.com&label=live%20on%20render&color=success) ![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/dsk-dev-ai/distrlab?label=release) ![stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/dsk-dev-ai/distrlab?color=gold) ![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/dsk-dev-ai/distrlab) ![svelte](https://img.shields.io/badge/Svelte_5-FF3E00?logo=svelte&logoColor=white) ![typescript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-3178C6?logo=typescript&logoColor=white) ![vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-646CFF?logo=vite&logoColor=white) **Status:** v1.1.0 — live on Render, in review as a PR. Circuit breaker + two smarter LB strategies join the seven original scenarios. 100% in the browser: no backend, no LLM, no paid API, no tracking. Everything runs inside a Web Worker on a static page — works offline, deployable to any static host.
## Why DistrLab? | Pain point | DistrLab solves it | |---|---| | Static diagrams that you just nod along to | A **live topology you can actually break** — every toggle moves real latency, error and throughput numbers | | Tutorials that only show the happy path | **Eight failure scenarios**: stampede, backpressure, throttling, LB skew, partition, stale replicas, a tripping circuit breaker | | "I get it" fading an hour later | **Hands-on memory** — break it, watch it recover, then re-check yourself | | Trusting that health checks / least-inflight work | **See requests reroute around a dead instance in real time** | | Taking load balancers on faith | **Round-robin vs random vs P2C vs least-latency** head-to-head against a weak instance | | Paid doorstopper simulators | Free, offline, no signup — a Svelte 5 + Canvas + Web Worker static page | ## Contents - [A taste of the action](#a-taste-of-the-action) - [Scenarios](#scenarios) - [Controls](#controls) - [How the simulation works](#how-the-simulation-works) - [Development](#development) - [Deploy](#deploy) - [Roadmap](#roadmap) - [Support](#support) - [License](#license) ## A taste of the action A healthy, idle playground — p95, throughput, capacity, queues and cache hit ratio all visible at a glance: ![healthy playground](media/distrlab-playground.png) Same cache expiry, **single-flight off**: every request herds at the origin and the catalog service melts down: ![cache stampede: expired cache without single-flight melts down the catalog service](media/distrlab-stampede.png) The same expiry with **single-flight on**: waiters coalesce at the cache and the catalog stays idle: ![the same expiry with single-flight on: waiters coalesce, the catalog stays idle](media/distrlab-coalesced.png) A real run, compressed — expire the cache, watch it recover: ![Demo](media/distrlab-demo.gif) ## Scenarios | # | Scenario | The lesson | |---|----------|-----------| | 1 | Playground | A healthy baseline: p95, throughput, capacity, queues, cache hit ratio | | 2 | Cache stampede | Turning off single-flight near a TTL expiry herds every request at the origin | | 3 | Queue backpressure | Shallow queues shed fast; deep queues trade errors for latency (both hurt) | | 4 | Rate limiting | A token bucket in front of the service protects it, at the cost of 429s | | 5 | Load balancer strategies | Round-robin vs random vs least-inflight vs sticky vs P2C vs least-latency under skew and failure | | 6 | Network partition | A cut link stops traffic; health checks + least-inflight route around it | | 7 | Replication lag | Reading a replica is fast and stale; tune the lag and watch stale reads | | 8 | Circuit breaker | A breaker in front of a flaky dependency: slow timeouts → instant 503s, then probe back to health | ## Controls - **Buttons in the header** switch scenarios, reset, pause, and set sim speed (space / `R` / `1`–`8` keyboard shortcuts). - **The graph** is the live topology — click a node to open the Inspector, drag to rearrange, scroll to zoom, drag the background to pan. - **Knobs** in the sidebar change arrival rate, capacities, queue limits, TTL, single-flight, LB strategy, health checks, timeouts, replica lag, fault windows, and the breaker's trip threshold / cooldown / probe limit. - **Inspector** can crash / restart a service, expire a cache, slow an instance, partition/repair links, and trip or reset the circuit breaker by hand. - **Charts** (bottom) track p95, throughput, error rate, queue depth, and cache hit ratio over time; the **insights panel** explains what's currently wrong. ## How the simulation works A discrete-time queueing model ticks every 20 ms of simulated time (player time is scaled 1×/2×/4×). Requests are small objects that carry latency, are counted against windows, drain through queues, wait in `proc` slots for a service time drawn from a log-normal distribution, and eventually complete or fail with `timeout | rejected | throttled | conn | crashed`. - **Services** have capacity (rps) and queue limits; over their limit they reject with 503. - **Client timeouts** kill in-flight requests; a request that dies mid-route still credits the target's error slice. - **Health checks** use an error-rate EMA with probe fallback; unhealthy nodes are pulled from LB rotation and get probed once per second, and their health recovers (decays) once the outage ends — so recovery is automatic. - **Least-inflight** counts what's *actually* waiting — including requests still travelling across the network, so a silent hole (partition) repels traffic. **P2C** picks the less loaded of two random candidates; **least-latency** prefers the node with the lowest response-time EMA. - **Circuit breaker** trips OPEN above a recent error-rate threshold, fast-fails with 503, goes half-open after a cooldown, and closes once its limited probes succeed. - **Cache** write-misses coalesce when single-flight is on; expiry refills the window. - **Rate limiters** are token buckets refilled per tick. - **Replica reads** are always served, but carry the configured staleness lag. ## Development ```bash bun install bun test # headless engine tests (no browser needed) bun run dev # vite dev server bun run check # svelte-check (types + a11y) bun run build # production build → dist/ bun run preview # serve the build locally ``` The engine is framework-agnostic (`src/sim/engine.ts`) and runs headless in a Web Worker (`src/sim/worker.ts`); the UI (`src/App.svelte`, `src/lib/`) is a thin canvas + Svelte skin over the snapshots it emits. AutoDeploy is on, so every push to `main` rebuilds. **Honest note:** `dist/` is 100% static with no server-side logic, so it can be dropped onto any static host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages…) — the SPA fallback is the only host-specific thing to configure. ## Roadmap - [x] v1.0.0 — live playground, 7 scenarios, inspector, charts, insights - [x] v1.1.0 — circuit breaker + scenario, P2C and least-latency LB strategies, engine test suite - [ ] v1.2.0 — chaos & retries: backoff with jitter, fault scheduler, per-request work log - [ ] v1.3.0 — share & export: scenario URLs, layouts, PNG/GIF export - [ ] v2.0.0 — beyond the single request path: sagas, quorum/consensus, multi-region, leader election See [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) for the full version-wise plan. ## Support Built by [@dsk-dev-ai](https://github.com/dsk-dev-ai).
